k557: Durrës city centre asks €1,900–2,800/m², the top of the city's range. The band covers the whole seafront strip — Currila, Vollga and Taulantia — rather than a single street, and penthouses on it go above €3,000/m². Currila alone is up 70–90% since 2019. Buyers here are mostly local families and Tirana commuters rather than seasonal investors, which is why the zone holds its price out of season. One thing to check before you sign: notary and tax costs are calculated from the state reference price, not from what you actually pay. Durrës still applies a single city rate; a 2025 draft that would have raised the port zone to 200,000 lek/m² has not been approved and is being revised.

k563: Farkë and Lundër sit south of Tirana around the TEG axis and hold the most expensive reference band in Albania: the Farka lake zone reaches 257,000 lek/m², roughly €2,620, four times what Paskuqan carries inside the same municipal field. This is not an apartment market, which is why it is quoted in whole prices rather than per square metre — Piccadilly at €690k for a three-bedroom, Rolling Hills Lake at €950k, Collina Verde between €950k and €1.3m, Farka Lake Shore from €1.22m to €1.73m. The tenant base is expatriate management on executive packages, and new gated schemes appear every few months, which is worth remembering before assuming scarcity will hold prices up on its own.

k570: Gjiri i Lalzit is the closest thing Albania has to a planned resort coast, and it is priced in tiers. Second line and early phases go at €1,500–1,700/m²; the established complexes — Vala Mar, San Pietro, Porto Lalëzi — sit at €2,500–3,500, with San Pietro having moved from €1,350/m² in 2021 to €2,800–3,650 in 2025. Above that it stops being an apartment market: townhouses run €600–850k, villas €900k–1.2m and first-line villas €1.5–3m. Buyers are the diaspora from Germany, Switzerland and the US plus wealthier Kosovars, and the honest summary from the research is that they came back here once the south passed €4,000–5,000/m². In peak season a 1+1 lets at €100–150 a night and a villa at €400–600.
k571: A planned resort bay north of the city, where the diaspora buys family luxury.

k577: Gjuhadol is one of Shkodra's historic quarters and it prices accordingly: a median €1,205/m² for new builds and €1,000/m² for resale in the August 2026 listing sample, or €1,200/m² across 19 listings. That sits below the centre and above Parrucë, close to the midpoint of the city's price gradient, with a new-build premium near 21%. Supply is genuine but thin, 79 apartment listings on MerrJep against 228 in Parrucë, so a buyer working to a narrow brief should expect to wait. Rental evidence for the quarter is too sparse to publish a yield. Figures are asking prices collected from listings in August 2026.

k584: Golem is the second and third line behind the beach south of Durrës, asking €1,100–1,500/m² and rising 8–15% year on year — cheaper than the first line, and cheaper than Qerret further down the same sand. The state reference price for the zone is €56,500 per unit, which is the figure your notary and tax bill are calculated from. The zone's standing problem is sewerage discharging onto the beach. It has not stopped prices, but it is the one thing worth checking on the ground, in season, before you buy here to rent out.

k593: Jonufër and Radhimë sit on the arc south of Vlora where the Lungomare promenade has been extending, and the extension is visible in the price: Radhimë went from €1,500–2,000/m² in 2024 to €2,000–3,000 — up 20–33% in a single year — with the agency survey putting the top of the whole stretch near €3,500. Before treating that as a trend, read what is inside it. Much of the 2024–25 move is an airport premium: Vlora International was meant to open, the concession has been tied up in a corporate dispute and SPAK charges, and as of summer 2026 there are no flights. The upside is real only if the airport actually starts; the downside is a correction in expectations that are already priced in.

k600: Kamëz is formally its own municipality on Tirana’s northern edge, and it prices like it: reservations in the Ulliri development’s first phase ran €750–900/m², the lowest figure anywhere in the agglomeration. Everything that makes it cheap is also what to examine — title history, transport into the city, and a reputation the area is still working against. The state reference rate is 62,500 lek/m², shared with neighbouring Paskuqan. This is a place to buy with a lawyer and a long horizon, not on a viewing and a good feeling.

k607: Kashar is Tirana’s western working edge — QTU, Tirana Business Park, warehousing — and its housing market follows the road rather than the city centre: €1,000–1,400/m² for new builds and €800–1,100/m² for resale. Diaspora buyers nearing retirement have been the steady demand here, drawn by space and the airport road. The two risks are the same thing seen twice: a lot of land, and a lot of it being built on at once, with the whole corridor competing for the same buyer. The Tirana–Durrës railway is the upside everyone quotes, and it has not carried a passenger yet.
k608: The Tirana–Durrës corridor: business parks, logistics, and a railway that has not opened yet.

k614:
Kavajë is the town behind the beaches south of Durrës. Golem, Mali i Robit and Qerret sit on its coast, but the town itself lies a few kilometres inland on the Durrës–Rrogozhinë road, with the railway, a market, schools, clinics and the everyday shops the beach strip lacks out of season.

Property here is a different market from the front line: apartments in the town at well below Golem prices, houses with a plot in the villages around it, warehouses and commercial buildings on the main road. It is the choice for a buyer who wants to live near the sea all year without paying for a sea view, or who needs land and space that the beach zone no longer has.
k615: Ten minutes from the sea and a year-round town: Kavajë is where the coast’s prices come down.

k620: Kombinat was built around a textile plant in the 1950s and still reads as a place with its own centre rather than a dormitory: new builds ask €1,000–1,300/m², resale €700–1,000/m², and a one-bedroom lets from €150–200 a month. It carries the lowest official reference rate in Tirana at 81,700 lek/m² — and the largest seven-year rise of any zone measured against it, up 151%, which is what early gentrification looks like in the numbers. Six kilometres from the centre is the price of admission. For a buyer who wants identity and a low entry point in the same purchase, there is not much else in Tirana that offers both.
k621: A 1950s factory town six kilometres out, and the cheapest real neighbourhood Tirana has.

k627: Komuna e Parisit is an upscale, quiet district next to the Grand Park, favoured by embassies, families and expats. It offers a family-oriented prime address without the noise of Blloku. As of 2026, off-plan units start around €3,000/m² near the Civil Aviation building, with completed stock around €2,700/m² (for example Haxhi Kika and the “White Tower”, up about 17% from their 2023 off-plan price). The main drawback is parking. It suits buyers looking for a calm, green, long-hold family home close to the centre with steady resale demand.

k633: Ksamil costs more per square metre than Sarandë — €1,800–3,000/m² — and earns less from short-term rental. The zone carries 522 listings, up 86% year on year, running at 38.3% occupancy: supply has grown far faster than the season has. Buying here on projected rental income alone does not work at these prices, and the arithmetic gets worse with every completion. The islands and the water are the reason to own in Ksamil; the yield is not. The state reference price runs €60,000–100,000 per unit, and that is the basis for notary and tax costs.
